title: AI-generated ‘doctors’ peddling fake cures on TikTok are a ‘huge danger’, experts warn

content_html:
The advice arrives in the confident cadence of a physician. Microwaving food in plastic gives you cancer, a spoonful of Coca-Cola mixed with onion will ease your pain, and a supplement called “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max” will fix your hair, nails, and joints in one go. The doctor delivering it does not exist.

A study published this month by Hallam, a UK digital marketing agency, found that AI-generated content appeared in 40% of the most-viewed health videos on TikTok, rising to 84% of the clips surfaced by searches for “health tips”. The researchers analysed 1,198 videos, and the top AI-generated ones averaged 2.5 million views apiece.

The findings land on a platform already thick with synthetic media. Nearly 60% of the videos TikTok shows new users are AI slop, a separate study found earlier this year, and dubious claims that AI outperforms doctors have already prompted warnings that patients could be misled at scale.

The doctors quoted in the research were blunt about the stakes. “Platforms like TikTok must do more to stop the rise of dangerous fake medical advice,” said Dr Emma Runswick, deputy chair of the British Medical Association council.

Professor Frankie Swords, NHS England’s national medical director, said many clinicians “are reporting an increasing number of patients who feel worried and confused due to false advice”.

Alex Ruani, a health misinformation researcher at University College London, was sharper still, describing the phenomenon as “industrialised exploitation of trust”.

The videos follow a recognisable template. A polished avatar, built with off-the-shelf tools, lip-syncs a script that blends plausible wellness tips with disproven myths and a pitch for a product that often does not appear to exist.

Hallam found no online trace of “Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max”, the anti-ageing remedy touted in one widely shared clip. Other clips recycle familiar cancer myths about microwaving food in plastic, deodorants, and sleeping near a phone.

The pattern is rarely accidental. Many of the accounts exist to sell something, whether a branded supplement, an affiliate link, or a subscription, and the fabricated white coat is what does the persuading. The polish is the point, and so is the plausibility.

This is not the first alarm. In February, the non-profit Science Feedback identified 18 such accounts within hours, several with hundreds of thousands of followers and videos reaching 14 million views.

The avatars claimed that turmeric lowers high blood sugar and that raw cacao and beetroot “unclog your arteries”, while pushing unproven supplements. Some cloned the faces of real physicians without consent, the kind of fakery that has spawned a small industry in deepfake detection.

The scale has unsettled the medical establishment on both sides of the Atlantic. John Whyte, chief executive of the American Medical Association, warned in February that scammers were cloning “the faces and voices of real, credentialed physicians” and called for physician identity to be treated as a protected professional asset.

He noted that one doctor’s own mother had been taken in by a fabricated video featuring her daughter, a measure of how convincing the clips have become. The same tools that promise gains in AI-assisted healthcare are now being turned against the patients they were meant to serve.

TikTok disputed the research. It said the findings came “from a marketing agency with commercial interests” and were “not an accurate reflection of our platform”, adding that it removes harmful health misinformation and partners with the World Health Organization and the NHS.

Its rules already prohibit both impersonation and misleading AI-generated content, and Science Feedback’s investigation noted that the company takes down most violating material proactively. The gap is between the policy and the feed.

The detection tools are improving, but the economics run the other way. One video app alone reportedly generates around 3 million clips a month, and accounts pulled for impersonation have been seen reappearing within the hour. The doctor may not be real, but the supplement sale is.

英国国民医疗服务体系（NHS）国家医疗主任弗兰基·索兹（Frankie Swords）教授表示，许多临床医生“报告说，越来越多的患者因错误的建议而感到担忧和困惑”。

伦敦大学学院的健康错误信息研究员亚历克斯·鲁阿尼 (Alex Ruani) 的观点更为尖锐，他将这种现象描述为“对信任的工业化利用”。

这些视频遵循可识别的模板。 一个用现成工具构建的精致化身，对口型同步脚本，将看似合理的健康秘诀与已被证实的神话和对通常不存在的产品的宣传融为一体。

哈勒姆在网上没有发现“Hyalethinap Plus Pro Max”的踪迹，这是在一个广泛分享的视频中吹捧的抗衰老药物。 其他剪辑则重复了人们熟悉的关于癌症的神话，比如用微波炉加热塑料食品、除臭剂以及睡在手机旁边。

这种模式很少是偶然的。 许多帐户的存在是为了销售某种东西，无论是品牌补充剂、附属链接还是订阅，而捏造的白大褂就是起到说服作用的。 润色是重点，合理性也是重点。

这不是第一次警报。 2 月份，非营利组织 Science Feedback 在数小时内识别出 18 个此类帐户，其中几个帐户拥有数十万粉丝，视频观看次数达到 1400 万次。

这些化身声称姜黄可以降低高血糖，生可可和甜菜根可以“疏通动脉”，同时推销未经证实的补充剂。 有些人在未经同意的情况下克隆了真正医生的面孔，这种造假催生了深度造假检测的小产业。

这一规模让大西洋两岸的医疗机构感到不安。 美国医学会首席执行官约翰·怀特 (John Whyte) 今年 2 月警告称，诈骗者正在克隆“真实、有资格的医生的面孔和声音”，并呼吁将医生身份视为受保护的专业资产。

他指出，一位医生的母亲被一段以她女儿为主角的捏造视频所迷惑，这可以衡量这些视频的可信度。 那些承诺在人工智能辅助医疗保健方面取得进展的工具现在却被用来对付它们本应服务的患者。

TikTok 对这项研究提出异议。 该公司表示，调查结果“来自一家具有商业利益的营销机构”，“并不能准确反映我们的平台”，并补充说，该公司消除了有害的健康错误信息，并与世界卫生组织和国民医疗服务体系（NHS）合作。

它的规则已经禁止假冒和误导性的人工智能生成内容，《科学反馈》的调查指出，该公司主动删除了大多数违规材料。 差距在于政策和饲料之间。

检测工具正在改进，但经济却相反。 据报道，仅一款视频应用程序每月就会生成约 300 万个剪辑，并且因冒充而被撤回的账户在一小时内又重新出现。 医生可能不是真实的，但补充剂销售是真实的。
